verdicts.conflict: Whether federal pre-deployment licensing gates are necessary to prevent catastrophic biological or cyber dual-use failures despite their market-concentrating effects.
verdicts.rationale: Neither side presents decisive empirical proof reconciling the catastrophic tail risk of dual-use models against the quantifiable harms of delayed medical innovation. The safetyist position highlights severe theoretical risks from unconstrained training runs, while the accelerationist position correctly identifies real opportunity costs in healthcare. The debate remains deadlocked because both outcomes carry high-severity, low-visibility probabilities.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Quantified empirical data from a controlled sandbox demonstrating whether pre-deployment delays actually prevent specific biological or cyber attacks.

verdicts.conflict: Whether regulatory agencies can effectively implement adaptive runtime telemetry and compliance audits for advanced AI without stifling open-source developer ecosystems.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist argument logically exposes a fatal flaw in the historical analogy between static medical software and recursive frontier models. Because frontier models use internal fine-tuning that outpaces static post-market audits, traditional compliance models fail to monitor decentralized deployment. The skeptic analogy to FDA Software-as-a-Medical-Device fails because clinical software does not recursively self-modify.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that decentralized open-source toolchains can support automated, tamper-proof runtime monitoring without centralized gatekeepers.
